title: Self Host Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Setup Guide (2026)
summary: Self-host Nemotron 3.5 Bolt with the 24GB variant for local deployment. Memory requirements stay predictable even at longer context lengths.
body_markdown:
## Connecting a self-hosted model to an Activepieces workflow


Because Activepieces has no native Nemotron 3.5 Bolt support, you connect your self-hosted copy through one of three routes, and the plainest of them is an HTTP request step.


Evidence of your own is only useful if the model sits inside a flow you control. The first question for each route is who owns the connection: which account holds the endpoint URL and the API key it checks.


Hosting the weights yourself is a decision about control, and the platform around them shouldn't quietly give it back. Most vendors monetise control by shipping a stripped self-hosted build, but Activepieces doesn't hold anything back from the buyers who need it most.


> Hosting the weights yourself is a decision about control, and the platform around them shouldn't quietly give it back.


SSO, SCIM, custom RBAC, audit logs, release management and secret manager integration all run in the air-gapped edition as they do in the managed cloud.


MoneyGram and Moneypenny run Activepieces in production, and you can confirm the match by laying the enterprise feature list in the air-gapped docs beside the cloud's.


We haven't run the model ourselves, so treat what follows as a wiring plan to test, not a report of results.


Aim for the shape in the screenshot below.


It's a four-step flow named "Test Flow" in which a schedule trigger starts a code step, an HTTP request fetches data, and an agent step, currently selected with its configuration panel open, writes from a long prompt that references the earlier steps by variable.


Notice that the agent's prompt pulls in outputs from the steps before it, which is exactly how your model's reply will be passed on to later steps. The next three options differ only in which kind of step stands where the model call sits.


### Option 1: HTTP request step


Start here. If your serving software exposes an OpenAI-style chat endpoint, which is a setting to confirm in its own documentation, the HTTP request step can post a JSON body containing the model name and one message to it.


Put the key in an Authorization header as a bearer token, and store it in an Activepieces connection rather than pasting it into the step, so the credential has one named owner.


The reply comes back as JSON, and a later step reads the message text from its path in that response.


### Option 2: AI step with an OpenAI-compatible provider


If your Activepieces version lets you register a custom provider with a base URL and key, the AI step can call your server and spare you hand-built requests. Check that the setting exists in your edition before you plan around it.


You see the output, not the raw request, and that makes debugging harder on a new model. That is the trade-off.


### Option 3: an MCP server


This is the most work. An MCP server would wrap the model as a tool that an agent step calls on its own.


Use it only once the first two routes work, because it adds a second service to maintain and a second set of credentials to assign an owner to.


Finish with the smallest useful flow, whichever route you pick. It has one trigger, one prompt sent to the model, and one step that uses the reply, such as writing it to a document.


When that runs end to end, you have a baseline for everything else.
